item.title: U.S. Army Member Arrested in Britain on Suspicion of Spying for Russia
item.description:
Britain’s counterterrorism police said on Tuesday that they had arrested a member of the U.S. Army on suspicion of spying on behalf of Russia after a joint investigation with the F.B.I. and U.S. military intelligence.

The 41-year-old man was arrested near Gloucester, England, about 100 miles west of London, and was in custody pending possible charges, officials said.

Officials did not name the man but said in a statement that he had been detained on suspicion of violating Section 1 and Section 3 of Britain’s National Security Act 2023. Those sections relate to obtaining or disclosing protected information and assisting a foreign intelligence service. The police did not offer any other details, including about what the man was suspected of having done.

But Brig. Gen. Sean Stinchon, the commanding general of the U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command, said in the police’s statement, “The alleged conduct of a senior soldier, entrusted with sensitive information, is a sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent.”

In the police statement, the F.B.I.’s director, Kash Patel, is quoted as saying, “This important arrest involves allegations of espionage, which is of the utmost concern to the United States and our allies.”

Mr. Patel added, “While this investigation is continuing, I want to send a clear message — this F.B.I. has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath to the United States and whose actions endanger our national security and that of our partners.”

The Metropolitan Police also said in a statement, “The country to which the allegations relate is Russia.”

The Kremlin did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The man arrested was based out of the Imjin Barracks at the headquarters of NATO’s Allied Rapid Reaction Corps in Gloucestershire, according to a U.S. military official who was briefed on the case and spoke on the condition of anonymity in order to discuss sensitive information. The base is NATO’s largest in Britain and hosts troops from 20 allied nations responsible for rapid response to crises in the alliance.

The counterterrorism police in Britain have investigated several high-profile terrorism cases related to the United States in the past months, including two cases of arrests near air bases in England where the American military operates.

In September, five men were arrested and then later released on bail near R.A.F. Fairford in southern England. Two Latvian men were arrested in October on suspicion of a national security offense after breaching the perimeter of R.A.F. Molesworth, about 70 miles north of London, in Cambridgeshire, England.

In the statement on Tuesday, the police said the arrest of the U.S. Army member on suspicion of espionage was “not linked to any other ongoing Counter Terrorism Policing investigations.”

Valerie Hopkins and Michael Schwirtz contributed reporting.

item.title: On Dakar’s Packed Beaches, Africa Welcomes Its First Youth Olympics
item.description:
Teenage athletes from all over the world have descended on Senegal this month to compete in Africa’s first ever Olympic events, the 2026 Youth Olympic Games.

And in Dakar, Senegal’s sports-crazy capital on Africa’s westernmost tip, the locals are ready.

Fitness and athletic prowess have long been all-important here in Dakar. On any given day, ordinary young people put some of the world’s most toned muscles to work, wrestling, skateboarding, surfing and bike riding.

Women toting goggles and foam noodles make their way down alleyways to the sea to take part in mass early-morning water aerobics classes with energetic coaches.

Groups of men do synchronized calisthenics on the city’s public beaches, hopping backward in low frog jumps and coating themselves in fine sand after sets of push-ups.

Weight lifters lift homemade barbells formed by pouring concrete into buckets and sticking a piece of metal into it to dry.

And every evening, crowds gather up and down the city’s main coastal road — the Corniche — to run, lunge, jump and use the many outdoor gyms that have opened in the city in the past decade.

On a recent evening on Koussoum Beach, hulking men tied traditional loincloths around their waists and between their legs. Then they circled each other, pawing at each other’s hands like cats and pulling each other to the ground.

Beach wrestling is making its Olympics debut at the Games, delighting many in Senegal, where traditional wrestling is wildly popular. Traditional Senegalese wrestling has been practiced for centuries here, and in recent years has become extremely popular and lucrative for top-tier competitors.

“We’re going to beat everyone,” said Zale Baol, a sturdy, solemn-faced traditional wrestler on Koussoum Beach. “Gambia, Ivory Coast, Germany, the United States — everyone. We’re a country of wrestlers.”

He said the key to becoming a successful wrestler was very simple: enough training, and the right nutrition. In the morning, wrestlers should eat Dakar’s favorite breakfast street food, black-eyed pea sandwiches, he said. For lunch, thieboudienne — Senegal’s national dish of rice, fish and vegetables. And for dinner, couscous.

On a recent morning in Pikine, a satellite city on Dakar’s eastern edge, young hopefuls for the beach wrestling team sat on the steps of the national wrestling arena, a Chinese-built outdoor venue decorated with bas-reliefs of wrestlers. They were bracing for the day’s endurance training.

“I’ve been wrestling as long as I can remember,” said Abdoulaye Diouf, 17. He reminisced about how his community used to organize competitions for young wrestlers, rewarding the winners with mangoes.

He winced as he recalled his mother’s wrath when he skipped school to compete in a match. But, he said, “I’ve always been stubborn.”

Dakar and the other two cities hosting Olympic events this year have undergone makeovers in recent weeks ahead of the Games. At the newly renovated Iba Mar Diop Stadium, men shoveled gravel until the last minute.

Many Senegalese were delighted by the new works, saying it was good for a struggling economy, and particularly good for the city’s huge cohort of young people.

“Africa has begun to develop,” said Moussa Thiam, an amateur boxer, on a recent evening.

For some of Dakar’s young athletes, though, the Games remained out of reach.

Over in Ngor, a fishing village of winding alleyways and colorful boats in Dakar, children of all ages glided along rails at Deggele skate park. The park was founded by Moussa Mbengue, who pioneered skateboarding in the area in the 1990s, after a French surfer gave him a board.

Ngor’s most promising young skateboarders, the 15-year-old twins Aminata and Mamadou Samb, had hoped to participate in the Games. Unfortunately, they could not leave the country to attend training sessions that might have enabled them to qualify, according to Mr. Mbengue, their trainer, and Awa Fall, the head of Senegal’s skateboarding federation.

Mr. Mbengue and Ms. Fall each had a different explanation for why the twins were unable to go, and each blamed the other.

But “we are not discouraged,” Mamadou said playfully. “No one in Senegal is better at skateboarding than us.”

Ahead of the Games, few young Dakarois knew how to get tickets to the events, or even what sports would be played.

“I’m only interested in soccer,” said Malick Ndiaye, 17, who had finished school for the day and was on his way to his father’s electronics store in the market. He was pleased to learn that futsal, a fast, indoor version of soccer, would be played.

During an opening ceremony, visitors were transfixed by the choreography, and the voice of the singer-songwriter Baaba Maal blaring from speakers. Lively recreations of Senegalese street scenes showed people selling coffee and fruit.

But away from the venues, Dakar kept up its own routines.

Runners jogged up and down the 198 steps to the city’s giant African Renaissance Monument, depicting a bronze family gleaming in the morning sun.

Others stretched on the sidewalk overlooking the turquoise waters of the Atlantic Ocean and one of Dakar’s most famous buildings, the windswept Divinity Mosque.

“Every country should pray to host the Olympics,” said Zale Baol, the traditional wrestler.

Saikou Jammeh contributed reporting.

item.title: This Defense Makes Drones (and GPS) Think They’re in Peru
item.description:
The S.U.V. in front of us suddenly pulled over. The driver had been trying to lead us to antennas near Kyiv, the Ukrainian capital, that scramble the signals of Russian drones and missiles, but his GPS had gone haywire.

“Apologies. Some technical issues,” texted Serhii, a spokesman for Cascade Systems, the Ukrainian defense company that made the system. He asked that only his first name be used, out of concern for his safety.

We should have known: The S.U.V.’s navigation system had decided that the vehicle was in Lima, Peru, 7,628 miles southwest of Kyiv.

This happens all the time to Ukrainians. When Cascade’s antennas are switched on to misdirect Russian bombardments, the GPS in phones and cars is often misdirected, too — to that particular South American city.

This was now happening to a few of the very guys behind the mapping chaos. They had been hoisted on their own antennas, so to speak.

The system, called Lima for obvious reasons, blasts out electromagnetic interference meant to strip the eyes and ears from Moscow’s missiles and drones, making them think they are somewhere else.

Sometimes, the weapons are so confused to be in Peru that they make severe turns and break apart midair. This has happened even to Russia’s powerful hypersonic missiles, Cascade and Ukrainian military officials say.

But the Lima network has also rewritten the map for getting around Kyiv, suggesting that in any place that deals constantly with drones and electronic warfare, the days of accurate GPS could be numbered.

We were determined to see why, even if we couldn’t figure out where we were.

It’s easy to get sent to Lima.

A colleague’s ride-sharing app told her she would be dropped off at her Kyiv home in 12,276 minutes, after driving across South America, the Atlantic Ocean and much of Europe.

A Ukrainian government official’s Garmin GPS watch said he had run 6.22 kilometers in Lima in 15 minutes 38 seconds, a pace that would make him one of the fastest distance runners ever.

A friend went onto the dating app Grindr to see matches in Kyiv, only to be greeted by men in Spanish. “I’m from Lima and you?” one asked.

Phones don’t always take their owners all the way to Peru. The GPS might put someone in a forest in neighboring Belarus instead of their apartment. On the east side of the Dnipro River, which divides Kyiv, people have found themselves in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

GPS confusion in Ukraine started years ago, when the military first started jamming drones. But it became a bigger problem in August, when the Russians began launching more daytime attacks. On one day in September, alarms in Kyiv lasted for 20 hours. So did the GPS wonkiness.

Increasingly, people are buying paper maps, downloading offline maps that rely on landmarks or trying other hacks.

Lima has become a verb. Food-delivery drivers are Lima’d. Cabdrivers are often Lima’d, especially the ones driving Teslas, which rely heavily on accurate GPS data to manage their core functions.

We got Lima’d on a September evening in rural Ukraine after conducting some interviews. As we drove at a sensible 38.5 miles an hour, an air raid alarm sounded. Suddenly, the Toyota Land Cruiser’s dashboard GPS showed us flying above Peru at 167 miles an hour, about to land in the country’s capital.

Got a confidential news tip? The New York Times would like to hear from readers who want to share messages and materials with our journalists.

Traffic in Kyiv is often snarled, in part because drivers who resettled from other besieged parts of Ukraine do not know how to get anywhere without GPS. When an air raid went off during a recent taxi ride, the driver, Serhii Semerenko, 56, frantically asked about our destination and route. He also tried to memorize his phone map.

“In a moment, all of this is going to disappear,” Mr. Semerenko said. He added: “We’re in Lima every day. And now you and me are about to be in Lima, too.”

This can mess with the most mundane modern conveniences. Ordering an Uber is easy, but finding it is next to impossible. You miss messages sent by your editor in Kyiv’s morning, because it’s the middle of the night in Lima and your phone has gone into sleep mode. (Seriously.)

Ukrainians love a good meme, and Lima is very memeable. People post screenshots of maps showing their locations — often featuring their Garmin running route, which is typically an inexplicable red circle near downtown Lima.

“After the war, I will buy tickets to Peru and I will definitely run around the Great Ukrainian Circle in Lima,” one man wrote.

To get to the bottom of this, we met in mid-October with the commander of the military’s Night Watch unit, who goes by the call sign Alchemist.

Cascade Systems started working on its antennas almost four years ago. Night Watch, a territorial defense unit in the Kyiv region, partnered with Cascade, suggesting tweaks and upgrades.

Early attempts scrambled some Russian cruise missiles and drones. The Russians then figured out ways to get around the jamming, largely by adding more antennas to their drones and missiles, said Alchemist, who for security reasons asked to be identified by only his call sign.

And so it has gone, this war of technology in which each side tries to out-jam the other.

By 2024, Lima was incorporated into Ukraine’s broader electronic warfare network. The latest version, Lima Quant, debuted in Kyiv in August 2025, when Night Watch set up the powerful antennas around the capital to create a networked polygon-shaped dome of electromagnetic noise, Alchemist said.

Cascade Systems and Night Watch eventually decided to trick GPS systems into thinking they were specifically in Lima, instead of confusing signals in a more general way. The goal was to distinguish the system from other electronic warfare efforts in Ukraine, which they said were claiming undue credit.

“We simply changed the signal and activated an Easter egg that had been hidden in the system from the very beginning,” Alchemist said, almost gleefully.

The team initially tried to create separate fake GPS coordinates, known as spoofing, for every major Ukrainian city. One would be spoofed to the Tower of London, another to Mount Everest. “We had the Avenue of the Baobabs in Madagascar, and other places we’d either visited or dreamed of visiting,” Alchemist said.

But eventually the team settled on Lima for all areas covered by the system in Ukraine. It was as good a city as any, and it was very far from Kyiv. It was also now a calling card.

Cascade Systems said Lima diverted more than 30 cruise missiles and 10,000 drones in the first three months of this year. Of 62 ballistic Kinzhal missiles launched into areas covered by Lima Quant, 33 broke apart in midair, Alchemist said. Others were diverted from their targets.

It is not possible to independently verify those numbers. Reports from the Ukrainian Air Force at the time mentioned that some missiles “did not reach their targets,” code language for electronic warfare. Alchemist showed us photos of Kinzhals split into pieces.

Lima’s biggest achievement, he said, came on May 24, when two Oreshnik supersonic missiles were fired toward the Kyiv region. Russia has claimed that the Oreshnik, its newest and most expensive missile, moves so fast that American-made Patriot interceptors cannot stop it.

A Night Guard member used the Lima Quant system to counter the missiles, after warnings from U.S. intelligence about an impending launch, Alchemist said. The first Oreshnik hit garages in the Kyiv region miles from any military target. The second split apart and landed in Russian-occupied territory, Alchemist said. Russia now appears to have mothballed both the Oreshnik and the Kinzhal.

Alchemist invited us to see Lima in action. And that is how we found ourselves behind a Lima’d S.U.V.

Eventually, we ended up in a field where we were ushered, almost reverently, to six Lima Quant antennas. They looked unremarkable.

“There is nothing more interesting for you to see here,” said a commander of a battalion inside the Night Watch unit, Max, who gave us an extremely short tour (and spoke on the condition that we use only his call sign).

The men in the field said they had never been seriously Lima’d. At any rate, they said, the system’s benefits outweigh the costs, an especially convincing argument as Ukraine faces shortages of Patriot interceptors.

Still, there is no denying the inconveniences. One Night Watch member, who uses the call sign Chameleon, told his colleagues about a friend whose new BMW had suddenly demanded a mechanic’s attention.

“It stopped in the middle of nowhere,” Chameleon said. “It said he drove the whole way from Lima, 10,000 or so kilometers, without changing the oil.”

item.title: Judge Allows Trump’s Defamation Suit Against BBC to Proceed
item.description:
A federal judge in Florida on Tuesday allowed President Trump’s defamation lawsuit against the BBC to proceed, rejecting the British broadcaster’s bid to dismiss it.

Mr. Trump sued the BBC over its documentary “Trump: A Second Chance?” which aired a week before the 2024 presidential election. The program spliced together two portions of remarks that Mr. Trump delivered roughly 55 minutes apart on Jan. 6, 2021, giving the impression that he was encouraging his supporters to storm the U.S. Capitol.

Mr. Trump’s legal team has accused the BBC of “intentionally, maliciously and deceptively doctoring his speech” in an effort to interfere with the election, and is seeking $10 billion in damages.

The BBC has apologized, acknowledging that its editing gave “the mistaken impression that Trump made a direct call for violent action,” a controversy that prompted the resignations of its director general, Tim Davie, and news chief, Deborah Turness. But it says it was not evidence of a fundamental bias in the BBC’s news reporting and did not constitute defamation.

On Truth Social, Mr. Trump described Tuesday’s ruling as a “A Huge Victory against Fake News BBC.”

A spokeswoman for the BBC said in an emailed statement: “We are surprised by this decision but respect the court’s authority and note the case will now proceed to the next stage. We remain confident in our position and will continue to respond through the proper legal process.”

Lawyers for the BBC had sought to have the lawsuit dismissed, in part because the program was never aired in the United States.

The judge, Jeffrey T. Kuntz of the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida, who was appointed to the bench by Mr. Trump, rejected that argument. He said that the BBC was a global organization that had marketed the program to Americans, noting that it had “emailed U.S. and Florida-based commenters with instructions on how to view the documentary.”

Judge Kuntz also rejected the broadcaster’s contention that the sequence in the documentary amounted to routine editorial trimming.

“BBC tries to frame this editing as ordinary editing done to condense a 70-minute-long speech into 12 seconds,” the judge wrote in the 40-page ruling. “But the court is not persuaded.”

“Editing is often required,” he continued. “However, given the time disparity between the two statements, the distance itself tends toward a plausible inference that BBC knew or should have known that the segment they were creating would not and could not have been a truthful statement.”

Addressing Mr. Trump’s broader claim that the BBC acted with “actual malice,” the legal standard required for a successful defamation claim by a public figure, Judge Kuntz wrote that “this does not prove BBC acted with actual malice. But it does make it plausible.”

The judge said that whether Mr. Trump can prove his claims at trial would be “left for another day.”

Judge Kuntz dismissed a secondary claim Mr. Trump made against the BBC, that it had breached Florida’s Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act.

Mr. Trump faces a Dec. 11 court deadline to sit for a deposition in the case.

item.title: A.I. and Market Whiplash
item.description:
Last week’s midterm elections were perhaps the first major elections fought at least in part over issues related to artificial intelligence. This year saw record donations from tech executives to tech-friendly candidates. And in some cases, A.I. was actually on the ballot: In local ballot initiatives across the country, people voted to limit or prevent the development of data centers. Many newly elected Democrats have promised A.I. regulation.

If A.I. has surged to the forefront of U.S. politics, it’s in part because A.I. is at the forefront of the U.S. economy. And stock markets around the world rise and fall with A.I. shares, particularly the multitrillion-dollar behemoths based in Silicon Valley. I spoke to my colleague Joe Rennison, who covers financial markets, about the dramatic swings in tech stocks following the midterms and what they mean — for Americans, and for the rest of us.

So, Joe. We’ve seen some serious volatility in the stock market after the midterms. First markets rallied, then they had their worst day in nearly two years. This week, as Nvidia stock plunged because of the Jensen Huang affair, the rest of the market bounced back.

What’s going on, and how much of all this is down to politics?

Certainly some of it is down to politics. The initial rally after the midterms came in part from investors who had parked their cash on the sidelines, in case of some unexpected event — say, a contested election. They bought back in when it became evident we were going to get a clear outcome.

The plunge the next day, though, came after some weaker than expected financial reports from a couple of A.I. companies, and after investors began processing what Democratic control of Congress and some Democratic wins at the state level might actually mean for the A.I. industry.

But markets have rallied since and now seem to be trying to find some equilibrium. I haven’t yet spoken to any professional investor who thinks we’re at the start of a more severe downturn. It’s more that perhaps the first leg of A.I. development, characterized by astronomical growth (and stock returns), may be slowing.

What are investors worried about?

Many people were already worried about the rapid growth in A.I. slowing down ahead of the midterms, and whether the huge amount of spending by A.I. companies would result in big profits any time soon.

Then the midterms hit, and it wasn’t just that Democrats won control of Congress. They won governorships in states that are important hubs for data centers, sometimes by running anti-data-center campaigns. And suddenly people really began to wonder if the rosy assumptions embedded in such lofty stock prices were still reasonable, or whether prices needed to come down a bit.

On regulation, voters seem to want it. But is the U.S. economy now so dependent on a handful of A.I. companies that even Democrats will have to think carefully about regulating A.I.?

I think that dependency is a real concern. Just 10 companies make up roughly 40 percent of the S&P 500, and so swings in the share prices of just a handful of big tech companies can move the entire market.

But it’s worth pointing out that most people who talk about more A.I. regulation or more scrutiny on A.I. tend to talk in terms of slowing down the industry, not stopping it entirely. Some analysts have actually argued that easing the rapid pace of growth would alleviate some of the strains on the American companies driving that growth, and would boost profits and bolster their positions as industry leaders. In other words, a more gradual pace of growth could be healthier in the long run for these companies and for the whole economy, even if it causes some short-term market pain.

How does the upcoming Anthropic I.P.O. fit into all this? It’s another blockbuster. What does its target valuation tell us?

Well, bankers had floated a $2 trillion valuation at one point; ultimately, Anthropic looks to be aiming for just (!) $1.4 trillion, at least for now. So it seems like some of the air has come out over the past couple of months, and that reflects a broader revaluation of public companies. But it’s still a highly sought-after I.P.O., with plenty of investor demand. That’s important because its size means its public debut is not just important to the A.I. industry but to the entire market.

And what about for the rest of the world? Other markets have also had a bumpy ride the last few weeks, right? How much do we all depend on U.S. tech companies, and U.S. politics?

There’s no shortage of examples of the U.S. economy and financial markets driving developments around the world. But in the case of A.I., it’s not just U.S. markets affecting the rest of the world, but also vice versa.

Japanese markets, because of low interest rates, have become a favorite place for investors to borrow money, which is then reinvested in U.S. stocks. Taiwan has the largest manufacturer of chips designed by U.S. tech behemoth Nvidia. And South Korean stock markets have become home to highly leveraged bets on baskets of A.I. companies.

South Korea’s Kospi index fell over 10 percent following the election result, before quickly bouncing back over 7 percent, underscoring how many places around the world have made big bets on A.I., and have a stake in what Democrats do next.

Nvidia’s board of directors was meeting late Wednesday U.S. time to discuss the future of Jensen Huang, the company’s chief executive. He is under investigation for having had an affair with Alice Huang, a woman who U.S. intelligence determined is a Chinese spy.

Earlier in the day, The Times reported that Huang had had another extramarital relationship with a Nvidia executive who reports to him, according to five people who worked at the company.

Huang’s potential exit would have widespread ripple effects and open an uncertain chapter for Nvidia, a linchpin of the A.I. boom. It controls an estimated 90 percent of the market for the computer chips used in the big A.I. projects that are driving the U.S. economy.

As the board deliberated Huang’s future, Nvidia’s share price plummeted.

As President Trump and China’s leader, Xi Jinping, prepare to meet next week to discuss trade, the Nvidia scandal has shown that behind their diplomacy is a fierce intelligence rivalry.

We’re a country of wrestlers.”

Max Worsley and his younger sister, Alicia, grew up steeped in their father’s love for Antarctica.

When the father, Henry Worsley, died in 2016, his death left unfulfilled a promise he had made: that he and Max would someday trek through Antarctica together. It would have been Henry’s next expedition, the trip that would solidify their father-son bond. This month, Max embarked on that journey into the lonely land his father loved. Once a titan of consumer electronics and manufacturing, Japan now earns more foreign revenue from overseas content than from traditional mainstays like semiconductors and steel. Sony, one of Japan’s most famous manufacturers, now earns 70 percent of its profits from entertainment, and the new chief executive sees anime as an alternative to the assembly line. item.title: Same-Sex Relations Decriminalized in Trinidad by a Court in Britain
item.description:
A ruling by a British-based court has invalidated laws criminalizing homosexuality in Trinidad and Tobago, setting a precedent for those challenging similar laws in other nations in the Caribbean and possibly beyond.

The ruling was handed down on Tuesday by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in London, which serves as the highest court of appeal for dozens of crown dependencies, overseas territories and former British colonies.

Five British judges unanimously upheld a 2018 decision by a lower court in Trinidad that had found two sections of the Caribbean country’s 1986 law targeting private, consensual same-sex relations to be unconstitutional. An appeals court in Trinidad had reversed the lower-court decision in 2025.

Trinidad’s attorney general had argued that the law preserved traditional family values in the country, and had leaned on a legal mechanism called “savings provisions,” which kept many laws from the British colonial era.

The decision delivered a hard-fought victory to advocates for L.G.B.T.Q. rights in Trinidad. Jason Jones, an L.G.B.T.Q. activist who had been a key plaintiff against the law since 2015, called the ruling a “vindication.” He said it would provide hope to young L.G.B.T.Q. people in his country who are living in fear of legal and societal discrimination.

Still, Mr. Jones noted ruefully, to challenge the colonial-era law, his lawyers had to seek intervention from a court based in Britain — decades after Trinidad gained independence, in 1962.

“We are a colonized people,” he said. “Why are we running to white people in London for our justice?”

Here’s what to know about the ruling.

During the colonial period, Britain imposed its system of laws across a global empire spanning nations in the Caribbean, Africa and Asia.

Many laws on the books in Trinidad and Tobago are left over from before the island nation of 1.5 million people left the British monarchy and became a republic in 1976. While laws criminalizing homosexuality in Trinidad stemmed from colonial-era legislation, they were amended to be even stricter in 1986.

Even as colonies became independent in the latter half of the 20th century, some retained deep economic, cultural and legal ties to Britain as part of an umbrella group of nations called the Commonwealth. It is made up of 56 members.

One of the vestiges of the British Empire is the Privy Council, which serves as the court of last resort for some of those nations. Caribbean countries have the power to leave the Privy Council system, said Téa Braun, chief executive of Human Dignity Trust, an international legal organization focused on eradicating anti-L.G.B.T.Q. laws. And many have done so, moving to regional bodies like the Caribbean Court of Justice.

Although the Caribbean court is headquartered in Trinidad’s capital, Port of Spain, the country has not made it the final court of appeal. And Prime Minister Kamla Persad-Bissessar has said she has no imminent plans to do so.

Ria Mohammed, a Trinidadian lawyer and director of the Caribbean Center for Human Rights, said it was “deliciously ironic” that a British-based court had helped invalidate colonial-era laws. But she noted that Caribbean judges had also been major players in enacting similar changes across the region.

Mr. Jones, 62, who moved to Britain at the age of 21, said he had been frustrated by a legal apparatus that required change to come from outside Trinidad. But he said: “I will use any tool to fight. If systems exist, you have to work within those systems to dismantle them.”

The ruling was a source of deep personal pride for Mr. Jones, but it was also celebrated by rights groups in Trinidad and beyond that had supported his efforts.

“This victory is more than a legal milestone,” Pride TT, an L.G.B.T.Q. rights group in the country, said on social media on Tuesday. “It is a reminder that everyone deserves to live with dignity, privacy and freedom from discrimination.”

Alex Farrow, chief executive of Kaleidoscope Trust, a British-based charity for L.G.B.T.Q. causes, said in a statement: “Horrifyingly, the number of countries criminalizing homosexuality has been increasing over the past two years. To see that number fall yesterday is a huge achievement.”

The prime minister and attorney general did not respond to requests for comment on the decision. But homosexuality remains deeply stigmatized in the country, and some religious leaders in the country expressed disappointment in the ruling.

“I cannot tell anybody how to live their life,” Ellis Burris, president of the country’s Inter-Religious Organization, said in a phone interview. But he said he believed that homosexuality was “against the divine law.”

The ruling will not automatically cause anti-gay laws to be struck from the books in Trinidad, said Ms. Braun, the Human Dignity Trust executive. But she said they were now void and unenforceable.

And she said the ruling could be cited in challenges to similar laws in other countries that operate under the Commonwealth system, though its effect would be “persuasive, not binding.” Each nation has its own constitutional provisions.

Challenges to laws in, for example, Jamaica, Grenada, Guyana and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines could be bolstered by the Trinidad ruling, Ms. Braun said.

While Trinidadians were rarely charged under the laws, rights groups argue that striking them down helps insulate them from discrimination.

item.title: Pope Leo XIV Goes Home, Meeting Ghosts of His Past
item.description:
Just a year and a half into his papacy and less than a month after surgeons removed a lobe of his right lung, Pope Leo XIV, the first pontiff born in the United States, touched down in his homeland on Wednesday.

Yet instead of setting foot on American soil, he arrived in Peru, where he spent two decades as a missionary, priest and bishop and became a citizen in 2015.

“Today I understand how much of this land remains with me and how much of my own story also belongs to you,” Leo said, speaking on Wednesday evening to Peru’s president, civic leaders and diplomats at the Gran Teatro Nacional, a theater and concert hall in the country’s capital, Lima. One of his biggest applause lines was when he referred to Peru as “my homeland.”

Having turned out record crowds at Masses in Argentina, the pope flew from Buenos Aires to Lima on Wednesday afternoon, reaching the final country of his 12-day tour of South America. The pope emerged at the top of the stairs next to a sign on the side of his plane that read “Pontifex Maximus,” and was greeted by Peru’s president, Keiko Fujimori, and a chorus of singing children on a red carpet at the Callao Air Base near Lima.

As his motorcade made its way through city streets under gray skies, about 3 million people lined the roads, according to local authorities, holding up cellphones as they waited for a glimpse of the pontiff.

His choice to visit Peru so soon after becoming pope — while deferring a visit to the country of his birth — underscored the deep emotional ties he feels to the place that formed him as a priest.

“That’s a connection that he doesn’t even have in Chicago at that level,” said Raúl E. Zegarra, assistant professor of Roman Catholic theological studies at Harvard Divinity School, referring to the city where the pope spent his childhood and attended seminary.

A ghost of the pope’s past hovered over his meeting with Ms. Fujimori, who was the first woman to be elected president in Peru in June and is the daughter of Alberto Fujimori, the dictatorial leader who ran the country for a decade and was convicted in 2009 of human rights violations, including murder.

When the pope was a young priest named Robert Prevost in Trujillo, in northern Peru, Mr. Fujimori dissolved Congress and suspended the Constitution. The Rev. John Lydon, a fellow Augustinian priest, served with the pope in Trujillo in the 1990s. He recalled that Father Prevost helped organize pro-democracy protests and recruited people to sign a petition supporting the 50th anniversary of the United Nations Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

As a bishop in the city of Chiclayo, where Leo will return on Friday, the pope told Father Lydon — now director of a leadership institute at Villanova University, the pope’s alma mater — that Mr. Fujimori “‘needs to ask pardon for all that he did.’” Mr. Fujimori died in 2024.

Standing at a podium on Wednesday next to Mr. Fujimori’s daughter, the pope seemed to hint at that history. “Past events deserve to be treated with justice and sensitivity, leaving room for harmony to grow and for differences to be addressed with respect,” he said.

In her welcome remarks, Ms. Fujimori, too, acknowledged the country’s painful history. Pope Leo’s visit “also calls us to reflect on our most urgent and pending task: national reconciliation,” she said. She added: “to move forward, Peru needs to reconcile. No country can live as a prisoner of its own wounds. We must learn to look back with truth and justice, but also with mercy and compassion.”

Unlike in the United States, where the pope voted in the midterm elections by mail, he did not vote in the Peruvian presidential election because “it was not possible,” he said to a reporter on the flight from Rome to Uruguay, the first leg of his trip.

Ms. Fujimori was elected this year as a conservative representing the political movement founded by her late father.

Marcela Rios Tobar, a political scientist and director for Latin America and the Caribbean at the International Institute for Democracy and Electoral Assistance, said Ms. Fujimori was a pragmatist who would “try to take as much advantage of this visit.”

Ms. Fujimori’s approval ratings have already fallen in the nearly five months since she was elected president, as voters have expressed dissatisfaction with the economy and crime. “She needs all the help that she can get to have her image boosted,” said Ms. Rios Tobar.

By the time the pope arrived in Lima, the visit had already become politically sensitive for the president. The opposition attacked her for announcing plans to leave for an economic summit in China on Sunday, missing the pope’s departure from Peru next Monday, and opposition lawmakers threatened to block her from leaving the country.

Ms. Fujimori told reporters in Lima on Tuesday that “it would never occur to me to slight our Pope,” but added that she could not miss a scheduled meeting with the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.

“My heart remains in Peru, but as president, I have state obligations to fulfill,” she said.

In Leo’s speech in Lima on Wednesday, the pontiff was not as pointed as he had been in Buenos Aires, when he seemed to implicitly criticize the economic austerity measures of President Javier Milei.

But he called on Peru’s government to recognize the dignity of work, the need for accessible health services and exhorted all members of the country’s democracy “to cultivate honesty, integrity, and a willingness to engage with others.”

Throughout his papacy, Leo has generally avoided direct criticism of governments, though he tangled with the Trump administration this year over the government’s conduct of the war in Iran.

Mr. Zegarra said that he was not surprised that the pope would temper his words in Peru. As a bishop, Leo was able to express his unvarnished opinions or protest publicly, but, Mr. Zegarra said, “what the pope tries to model as the head of the Catholic Church is to be a figure that can speak to all with decency, but also firmly.”

“He’s taking some distance from his documented history,” he added, “to try to be a bit more of a bridge builder.”

item.title: Strike on Gaza Hospital Kills at Least 6 and Injures 20, Rescuers Say
item.description:
An Israeli military strike on a hospital in the southern Gaza Strip killed at least six people and injured more than 20, according to a statement early on Thursday from the Civil Defense, Gaza’s rescue service.

The overnight strike hit a Nasser Hospital building in the city of Khan Younis, Mahmoud Basal, a spokesman for the rescue service, which is under the Hamas-run interior ministry, said in the statement. The New York Times is trying to verify who was killed in the attack.

The Israeli security agency and military said in a joint statement on Thursday that they had targeted Muhammad Abu Ismail, whom they identified as a Hamas commander “responsible for holding numerous hostages captive,” during the Gaza war.

The Israeli authorities said that Hamas had established a command center at the hospital complex to stage operations against Israeli forces and was storing weapons there. They added that steps had been taken to mitigate harm to civilians.

Hamas said the Israeli claim that the hospital was used for military activity was a “blatant attempt to justify a heinous crime targeting a civilian medical facility.”

In a statement, Gaza’s health ministry condemned the attack, calling it a “flagrant violation of international laws and conventions.” It did not respond to the Israeli claims.

The attack comes more than a year into a cease-fire between Israel and Hamas that has not brought an end to Israeli military strikes in Gaza and that has done little to alleviate the dire and deadly living conditions for the enclave’s two million residents.

Shortly after midnight, at least two missiles hit the roof of a four-story building in the hospital complex, penetrating the third floor and exploding on the second floor in the surgery department, Naseem Hassan, a paramedic and ambulance driver who works at Nasser Hospital, said by telephone.

Israel has continued to carry out frequent strikes in Gaza despite a U.S.-brokered cease-fire that Israel and Hamas agreed to in October 2025. More than 1,600 people have been killed by Israeli fire during the cease-fire, according to Gaza’s health ministry, which does not distinguish between civilians and combatants in its death tolls.

Nasser Hospital has been struck by the Israeli military multiple times since the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, prompted a devastating Israeli military response in Gaza. More than 74,000 people have been killed in the war, according to the health ministry.

In August last year, 20 people — including medical staff, rescue workers, patients and journalists — were killed in a strike on the hospital that drew a rare admission of error from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel, who called it a “tragic mishap.”

This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

item.title: A Key Paris Agreement Goal Is Dead. What Now?
item.description:
It was the climate movement’s unifying slogan for the past decade: “Keep 1.5 Alive.”

The tagline referred to the central ambition of the 2015 Paris climate agreement, in which almost every country pledged to try to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius.

Now, just 11 years after the target was set, 1.5 is effectively dead.

Scientists now say that without drastic efforts to reduce greenhouse gases, it is very likely that the planet will warm at least 2.6 degrees Celsius, or 4.7 degrees Fahrenheit, by the end of the century.

At COP31, the United Nations climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, diplomats who spent so long championing the 1.5 degree target lamented the abrupt setback.

“The world has no chance of holding to 1.5 degrees,” said Chris Bowen, Australia’s minister for climate change and energy, who is leading the negotiations.

Scientists for years have warned that allowing global average temperatures to rise 1.5 degrees Celsius, or 2.7 degrees Fahrenheit, above preindustrial levels would result in a profoundly more dangerous world. Extreme heat will become more common and more intense. Storms will become more powerful and destructive. Sea levels will rise. And poor countries will bear the brunt of the damage.

That scenario is already playing out around the world. In recent months, wildfires have raged from Canada to Indonesia. The collapse of a glacier in Nepal killed thousands and wiped away towns. Floods and mudslides devastated Brazil. And a European heat wave killed an estimated 50,000 people.

In the face of this mounting destruction, one lingering question at the climate talks was what would be the new goal, if any, as the world overshoots the 1.5 benchmark.

“We don’t think that there’s a new target,” said Ilana Seid, Palau’s ambassador to the United Nations. “We still have a Paris Agreement target of 1.5, and so we are still continuing to say that’s the target.”

Rachel Cleetus, director of the climate program at the Union of Concerned Scientists, warned against fixating on a new target, saying instead that it was important to confront what breaching the threshold has wrought.

“I don’t think it’s a question of replacing 1.5,” she said. “There is no new number. We are now in the unsafe zone.”

Leaders rejected the idea of resetting the goal to 2 degrees Celsius or even 2.5 Celsius, saying that allowing for endless revisions created a slippery slope that could make progress harder to achieve.

While world leaders acknowledged they had missed the target, they also said it might still be possible to get back to 1.5 degrees of warming.

The United Nations secretary general, António Guterres, called on countries to redouble efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions with the aim of limiting additional warming, and ultimately turning down the Earth’s thermostat.

“The truth is that we have the power to determine how high, how long and how devastating that overshoot will be,” he said. “We have the power to make sure the overshoot is a temporary breach, not a permanent sentence.”

In order for warming past 1.5 degrees to be temporary, humans would have to figure out how to lower concentrations of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere.

That won’t be easy. Emissions continue at near-record levels. Finding a path back to 1.5 degrees would require the world to drastically reduce the burning of fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas.

Although clean energy is growing rapidly, the world is expected to continue to use fossil fuels for decades to come.

Because reducing emissions is proving so difficult, some environmentalists and scientists are proposing different types of geoengineering, including large-scale carbon capture and storage or attempts to reflect the sun’s energy away from the planet by injecting particulate matter into the stratosphere.

“Overshoot must be kept as small and short as possible, and be rapidly reversed,” said Hilda Heine, president of the Marshall Islands, an island nation threatened by sea level rise. “We have fallen short of the emissions reductions needed to stay under 1.5. We must rewrite the future.”

Lisa Friedman and Chico Harlan contributed reporting.

Your newsletter host, David Gelles, spoke to the California governor on the sidelines of the climate summit in Turkey.

What can Democrats in Congress do on the climate front while President Trump is still in office? And what about House Resolution 1, the 2025 budget law that cut clean energy incentives?

I hope the Democrats make this part of their 100-day agenda. That it’s not just rolling back the worst cuts under H.R. 1, that we focus on restoring a lot of the good work that was done during the Biden administration under the I.R.A. and restore a lot of those cuts. Restore a lot of the cuts that were done environmentally in the infrastructure bill that was rolled back by the Trump administration. The clean energy subsidies and tax credits, the work on wind in particular that’s been attacked by the Trump administration, that should all be front and center on our agenda.

Do you think Democrats need to find new ways to talk about climate issues?

You can use different language, and that’s why I talk about places, lifestyles, traditions. That’s why we talk about extreme heat. That is why we have the extreme heat index in California. That is why we talk about climate risks and financial risks. Why we talk insurance markets. Why we just spent the day talking about wildfires and the impacts they’re having on our communities. So I think it’s our language, and for me the number one issue is the strategic imperative now to focus on this transition.

Any thoughts about 2028?

We’ll see. I mean, I still haven’t made a decision, so we’ll see how it all processes and plays out. But it’s all got fast-tracked. That was inevitable in some ways, unsurprising. But I think you’re going to start to see two or three debate stages set up in May and June of next year. And it’s already taking shape. It’s going to be fast.

Max Worsley grew up steeped in his father’s love for Antarctica. But when Henry Worsley died in 2016, he left behind an unfulfilled promise: that the two of them would one day trek across the continent together. This month, Max finally set out into the lonely expanse his father loved, to finish the journey on his own. — Raymond Zhong

item.title: Behind the Trump-Xi Bonhomie, a Fierce Spy War Rages
item.description:
As President Trump and China’s leader, Xi Jinping, prepare to meet next week to extend a fragile trade truce, a fresh espionage scandal has shown that behind their diplomacy is a fierce intelligence rivalry.

At its center is Jensen Huang, the Nvidia leader and an influential ally of Mr. Trump’s, who has acknowledged having an affair with a Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. intelligence officials suspect of spying for Beijing. China has denied the espionage allegation.

Under Mr. Xi, the Chinese Communist Party has built a more sophisticated and assertive spy service that regularly highlights the importance of technological security and of threats posed by the United States. At the same time, the Central Intelligence Agency has said that Chinese companies are a legitimate target for espionage in areas like artificial intelligence, semiconductors and biotechnology.

Nvidia’s computer chips power the global A.I. boom and sit at the center of Washington’s efforts to keep that technology out of China’s hands. That makes Mr. Huang, who has lobbied Mr. Trump to ease restrictions on the export of advanced chips to China, a prime target, analysts say.

“It is not at all surprising, given the centrality of Nvidia to U.S.-China tech competition, and the importance of tech competition in the overall U.S.-China rivalry, that someone like him would be a top target for Chinese intelligence collection,” said Sheena Chestnut Greitens, an expert on Chinese security at the University of Texas at Austin.

U.S. agencies concluded that the Chinese businesswoman, who goes by Alice Huang, was an asset of the Chinese Ministry of State Security. Nvidia has said that it is conducting an internal investigation. Ms. Huang has not responded to requests for comment.

“It is brazen, and yet I don’t think we should be surprised at all,” said Christopher K. Johnson, a former U.S. government intelligence officer who is now president of China Strategies Group, a risk consultancy. “Whenever the Chinese declare something a national strategic, whole-of-society priority, like they have done with chips and A.I., that implies they will use every tool available to them to work, buy or steal their way to that end.”

So far, the scandal has not apparently disrupted plans for Mr. Trump and Mr. Xi to meet next week in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen. Mr. Trump said on Monday that he did not plan to bring the matter up with Mr. Xi. He has repeatedly downplayed reports of Chinese spying and cyberattacks on the United States, arguing that Washington does the same.

That is a contrast with the Biden administration, which confronted China in early 2023 about a spy balloon that was spotted drifting across the continental United States. Official relations between the countries froze for months.

Mr. Trump’s approach could embolden China to take bigger risks, said Dennis Wilder, a former U.S. intelligence analyst on China and a senior fellow at Georgetown University.

“The president’s whole laissez-faire attitude toward spying reassures Beijing that the political blowback from espionage operations will be very manageable,” he said.

Mr. Huang was until recently also expected to travel to Shenzhen. When Mr. Xi visited the United States in September, the tech executive was a guest at the White House state dinner. He had joined a presidential trip to Beijing in May at Mr. Trump’s invitation.

“The president has over and over dismissed Chinese spying by saying that everyone does it,” Mr. Wilder said. “The problem is that no one else does it to the very damaging effect that the Chinese can and do.”

In recent years, Chinese spies have been accused of targeting the phones of American presidential candidates, recruiting U.S. Navy sailors, cultivating political aides, and planting malicious code in power grids and water systems that Americans rely on every day.

Beijing also has a history of ruthless counterintelligence operations. From 2010 through 2012, the Chinese government killed or imprisoned 18 to 20 of the C.I.A.’s sources in China, crippling American spying there for years, The New York Times reported in 2017.

Espionage has repeatedly strained relations, at times erupting into diplomatic crises, as when a U.S. Navy surveillance plane collided with a Chinese fighter jet in 2001 near China’s Hainan Island, killing the Chinese pilot. Beijing condemned Washington for spying and held the 24 American crew members for 11 days.

China’s lead intelligence agency, the Ministry of State Security, has transformed from a service that relied on gathering gossip at embassy dinner parties into a sophisticated spy shop that can go toe-to-toe with the C.I.A. with bigger budgets and modern tools like A.I.

Its political standing has risen as well. In 2022, Mr. Xi elevated the ministry’s then chief, Chen Wenqing, to the Communist Party’s Politburo, a council of the 24 most senior national leaders. He was the first spy chief in decades to ascend to that body.

The once-shadowy ministry has also stepped into public view, posting a stream of warnings on its WeChat social media account about foreign spies. It has publicized examples of Chinese nationals working for the government and a military contractor in Tokyo and Rome being recruited by C.I.A. officers to provide information about the government or the military.

At the same time, the United States has stepped up its intelligence gathering to include not just military and government targets, but also private Chinese companies, the deputy C.I.A. director, Michael Ellis, told a cybersecurity conference this year. Compared with past geopolitical rivals, China “poses a fundamentally different kind of threat to us because the competition is economic,” Mr. Ellis said.

The C.I.A. has also taken the unusual step of recruiting in public, producing a series of Mandarin-language videos urging disaffected Chinese officials to share secrets with the United States. (The Ministry of State Security’s WeChat account mocked the videos as “crude,” “farcical” and a sign of the C.I.A.’s “baffling incompetence.”)

In China, the case has drawn official denials and questions about what Beijing would stand to gain.

Ms. Huang had been an executive at a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed that buys advanced Nvidia chips. The United States began restricting sales of advanced chips directly to China in late 2022, but Chinese companies can lease computing power from data centers that use those chips in Southeast Asia, like the ones Megaspeed operates.

At the same time, China has also encouraged domestic companies to make do with less powerful domestically produced chips to promote greater national self-reliance, leading some analysts to question the significance of the Nvidia case.

“China does not want to import so many Nvidia chips,” said Shen Dingli, an international relations scholar in Shanghai. “They are trying to force Chinese companies to use Chinese chips from Huawei.”

The Chinese Foreign Ministry has rejected the espionage allegations surrounding Ms. Huang as “nothing but a smear against China.” On Chinese social media platforms, which are heavily censored, comments about Mr. Huang have centered on his extramarital affair.

Nationalist commentators in China have described the scandal as an effort that brings together American opponents of China, Mr. Trump, and artificial intelligence.

Ren Yi, a Harvard-educated Chinese blogger who goes by the pen name “Chairman Rabbit,” wrote: “Once again, anti-China politics weaves America’s disparate political causes together.”

Berry Wang contributed research.

item.title: Russia’s Ambassador to the U.S. Dies at 66
item.description:
Russia’s ambassador to the United States, Alexander Darchiev, who served during a rapprochement between the Kremlin and Washington, has died, the Russian foreign ministry said Wednesday. He was 66.

Mr. Darchiev died in Moscow of a “chronic illness,” Maria Zakharova, spokeswoman for the ministry, said in a statement published by Tass, the Russian state news agency.

“We have lost an outstanding diplomat, an experienced leader, a kind colleague and a mentor,” the ministry said in its statement. It described Mr. Darchiev as a “distinguished expert on the United States” who had “served in one of the most demanding areas of Russian foreign policy.”

Mr. Darchiev had been in the diplomatic service since 1992, and he was appointed as ambassador to the United States by President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia in March 2025.

His appointment came as President Trump sought to broker a cease-fire agreement to halt Russia’s war against Ukraine, which began in 2022. Mr. Darchiev’s term coincided with a thaw in relations between the Kremlin and Washington as U.S. policy shifted from staunch support for Ukraine under the Biden administration to pressure on Kyiv to make a deal with Russia.

In February last year, Mr. Darchiev led a Russian delegation meeting with U.S. officials in Istanbul about the operations of the two nations’ diplomatic missions. At the time he was director of the North Atlantic Department, a section of the Russian foreign ministry that oversees relations with Canada, Ireland, Britain and the United States.

“The dialogue on irritants has been ongoing, and certain improvements have been achieved,” Mr. Darchiev said last year in an interview with the Russian newspaper Kommersant in which he discussed frictions between the United States and Russia.

But he said the United States was tying discussions on certain issues, like Russian access to seized diplomatic properties in the United States, “with a settlement in Ukraine that suits its interests,” which he objected to.

Talks on ending the war in Ukraine, which had been stalled for much of this year, resumed this week in Abu Dhabi, the United Arab Emirates, after a push by the Trump administration that began in September. The discussions are not expected to yield fruit anytime soon.

It is not clear if Mr. Darchiev was involved in those talks.

Mr. Darchiev, who was born in 1960, graduated from Moscow State University in 1983. Information about his survivors was not immediately available.

Mr. Darchiev’s appointment to Washington as ambassador to the United States was not his first stint in the country or the region. He served as Russia’s ambassador to Canada from 2014 to 2020 and worked at the Russian Embassy in the United States from 2005 to 2010, according to a biography on the embassy’s website.

In the intervening years, Mr. Darchiev directed the North America Department and, briefly, the foreign ministry’s North Atlantic department, before serving in what proved to be his final role.

item.title: General Strike Ripples Across Spain Weeks Before National Elections
item.description:
Spanish workers staged a general strike on Wednesday for the first time in 14 years, protesting the rising rents and stagnant wages that have become central issues in the national election to be held this month.

Unions said millions of workers participated in the walkout, while hundreds of thousands of Spaniards joined rallies in Madrid, Barcelona, Valencia and other cities in the evening.

Early on Wednesday, protesters blocked roads in Madrid, set up picket lines outside major factories in Catalonia and disrupted transportation across Spain.

Police officers wielding shields and batons forced hundreds of demonstrators away from the Gran Vía, the central thoroughfare in Madrid, which rally goers had blocked. The anger of protesters in the capital was directed largely at “rentistas” — a Spanish term for people who live off rental income.

Later in the day, during a march through central Madrid that drew 120,000 protesters according to the government, demonstrators chanted in a festive mood, “One jump, two jumps, whoever doesn’t jump is a rentista.”

Clashes with the police erupted in Barcelona, where a group of masked protesters broke away from the crowd after the demonstration ended, according to local news media. The group smashed several shop windows, threw pyrotechnic devices at police officers and tried unsuccessfully to storm an Apple Store, the reports said.

The left-wing administration of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called for snap elections early last month, after the eviction in September of María del Carmen Abascal, an 87-year-old tenant in Madrid who became the face of Spain’s housing crisis.

Efforts by the government to enact legislation increasing tenants’ rights has failed to pass Parliament, blocked by opposition parties. Mr. Sánchez apparently hopes that frustration over that logjam will improve his chances in the vote, set for Nov. 29.

Mr. Sánchez’s government has been buffeted by damaging headlines over corruption scandals, a migration crisis and a deadly train crash late last month. Polls show that if the election were held today, his party and other left-wing allies would command fewer seats in Parliament than would a group of conservative parties.

The government has expressed support for the strike. “Every right that workers in this country enjoy was won through struggle and strikes,” Pablo Bustinduy, the social rights minister, said on Tuesday.

Workers say that low wages have left them increasingly squeezed out of cities, where rents are rising. Spain has a shortage of roughly 750,000 homes, according to the Bank of Spain, a figure projected to exceed a million by 2028. Over the past decade, rents in Spain have soared 87 percent, while wages have increased only 28 percent, according to El País, a center-left newspaper.

One of the unions that organized the strike on Wednesday, Comisiones Obreras, called the industrial action “a resounding success” that showed solidarity with young workers. But the main employers’ associations disputed the union’s estimates, saying that less than 5 percent of workers had participated in the walkout.

“In short, a failure,” they said in a statement.

A strike supported by a sitting government is somewhat unusual, a point not lost on parties opposing Mr. Sánchez’s bid for re-election. Alberto Núñez Feijóo, leader of the conservative Popular Party, said that the strike amounted to a campaign event against a potential right-wing government.

“It’s absurd,” he said on Monday, “a general strike against the opposition.”

Unions said the walkout was directed at local and national governments regardless of their political affiliation. “We don’t distinguish,” Valeria Racu, a spokeswoman for a tenants’ union, told the Spanish public broadcaster on Wednesday.

“We have no patience left,” she added. “The power is in the streets.”

item.title: Indonesia’s Vice President Resigns as a Political Alliance Unravels
item.description:
The vice president of Indonesia submitted his resignation to Parliament on Thursday, succumbing to a scandal about his academic credentials and injecting new political uncertainty in Southeast Asia’s largest economy.

Gibran Rakabuming Raka was elected as Indonesia’s youngest vice president in 2024, in a precipitous rise. He was a symbol of the partnership between his father, the outgoing president, Joko Widodo, and the incoming leader, Prabowo Subianto, that elevated Mr. Prabowo into office.

“The relationship has clearly fractured,” said Yoes C. Kenawas, a political analyst at the Indonesian Survey Institute. With Mr. Gibran’s departure, “Prabowo is attempting to demonstrate that he has stepped out from Jokowi’s shadow,” he added, referring to the former leader by his nickname.

Initially a political outsider, Mr. Joko came to be seen as a transformative leader of Indonesia. He helped rehabilitate the image of Mr. Prabowo, a former special forces commander who was discharged from the military for his involvement in the abduction and torture of pro-democracy activists under the dictator Suharto. To many, Mr. Prabowo was a reminder of the country’s authoritarian past. But Mr. Joko endorsed Mr. Prabowo as his successor, with Mr. Gibran running on the same ticket.

The alliance between Mr. Joko and Mr. Prabowo was cast as one of political continuity. Many voters had seen Mr. Gibran’s vice presidency as a way for Mr. Joko to continue his political influence.

“From the beginning, Gibran was brought on board solely to serve as a ‘vote-getter,’ rather than as an integral part of a unified leadership team intended to strengthen the performance of the Prabowo administration,” said Titi Anggraini, a lecturer of constitutional law at University of Indonesia.

Mr. Prabowo’s two years in office have been dominated by his authoritarian tilt and populist policies that have rattled the economy. In recent weeks his approval rating has plummeted, leaving the country in a combustible moment that evokes the ouster of Suharto three decades ago.

It was not immediately clear when Mr. Gibran’s resignation would be effective. He is stepping down after mounting calls for impeachment over allegations that he had failed to meet a requirement to run for office — holding the equivalent of a high-school diploma — even though he later earned a university degree.

Mr. Gibran has said that he finished grade 12 at a school in Australia. He has faced two cases, one that challenged his high school credentials and another that sought to remove him from office on the grounds that those credentials were illegitimate.

Last month, the Constitutional Court said that it had found no convincing evidence that Mr. Gibran possessed a foreign diploma equivalent to an Indonesian senior high school certificate. But it noted that it did not have the jurisdiction to unseat him directly.

Two weeks ago, the Supreme Court delivered another blow. It revoked a high school equivalency certificate that was issued to Mr. Gibran by the Education Ministry in 2019. But the justices did not establish that Mr. Gibran had forged a document, centering their ruling instead on administrative compliance.

Earlier this month, what appeared to be a seismic break in the Jokowi-Prabowo alliance emerged. Several officials, including Mr. Prabowo’s chief of staff, who were seen as close to Mr. Joko, were arrested on charges of wiretapping the president.

Mr. Joko appeared to cast a conciliatory note on Thursday.

“I have told Gibran that any position one holds is only temporary; positions are fleeting,” he told reporters. “We remain committed to supporting President Prabowo’s administration, especially regarding programs that benefit the broader public.”

The controversy that felled Mr. Gibran has an unusual family parallel.

Mr. Joko has faced claims that he doctored a university certificate to become eligible to run for office. Last week, Mr. Joko, appeared in a Jakarta courtroom to display his original diploma from Gadjah Mada University, seeking to rebut long-running allegations regarding its authenticity.

The Constitutional Court played a crucial role in Mr. Gibran’s ascendance to the vice presidency. In a 5-4 decision in 2023, it carved out an exception to the minimum age requirement of 40 for presidential and vice-presidential candidates, allowing younger candidates who had held elected regional office to run. Mr. Gibran, now 39, had been the mayor of the city of Surakarta.

The deciding vote was cast by Chief Justice Anwar Usman, who had been appointed by Mr. Joko and later married the president’s sister. Soon after, an ethics panel removed Mr. Anwar from his post, citing a conflict of interest, but it could not overturn the court’s decision.

item.title: A Sweaty, Muddy Jungle Trek to a Famed World War II Wreck
item.description:
Halfway through the morning, I’m being tossed around like a popcorn kernel in the back of a troop carrier playing an eclectic medley of Backstreet Boys and Papua New Guinean jams.

We’re traveling along what feels more like a collection of loose rocks, arranged to be roughly vehicle width, than a road. I’ve lost count of the number of river crossings, including one where the water lapped a few inches from the car’s windows. And this is during a dry spell.

Our caravan is headed for an unlikely tourist destination deep in the jungle on Bougainville Island, an autonomous region of Papua New Guinea in the Solomon Sea.

The piecemeal remnants of a Mitsubishi G4M1 — Betty, as the planes were code-named by the Allies in World War II — have remained for some 80 years at the crash site of Japanese Navy Adm. Isoroku Yamamoto. This is the spot where Admiral Yamamoto, mastermind of the Pearl Harbor attack, archvillain to Americans in the war, a respected and memorialized figure to the Japanese, met his end in 1943.

Bougainville was occupied by the Japanese in early 1942, in the months after Pearl Harbor, as the Imperial Navy pushed into the South Pacific, with Admiral Yamamoto at the helm. In April 1943, Allied forces intercepted and deciphered Japanese communication on the admiral’s travels, and American P-38 Lightning fighters gunned down his plane over southern Bougainville, a feat the Americans triumphantly dubbed Operation Vengeance.

Visiting the relic is not for one faint of heart, time or expense. And yet, war history buffs, Japanese pilgrims, a Chicago hot dog baron and lately, YouTubers, have made the journey, bringing a mix of curiosity, complicated feelings on war and, for many, the desire for bragging rights over going where few have gone.

So far, my journey has involved a flight to Port Moresby, the capital of Papua New Guinea, then a domestic leg to Buka, in the Autonomous Region of Bougainville. From there, it’s a ferry ride across a narrow strait, then four hours by rough, unsealed roads to the coastal town of Arawa. Then, another four hours by even rougher roads, up and over the fog-shrouded Crown Prince Range — to get to the start of the trek into the jungle.

I was in Bougainville with the photographer Matt Abbott to report on the region’s quest for independence, and the lasting legacy of a decade-long civil war that broke out in 1988. On our final day, we made a visit to Admiral Yamamoto’s plane.

I was curious why people would go to such lengths to reach the site. I imagined I might encounter Japanese visitors reflecting on their country’s legacy in World War II, or American or Australian tourists who knew of the place through family lore passed down by Allied servicemen.

As it happened, when I contacted Zhon Bosco Miriona, who runs Bougainville Experience Tours, the group scheduled to make the trip that day was made up of Chinese tourists.

So there we were in three cars — seven Chinese visitors, two journalists, a handful of guides and drivers — making our way to the crash site. As I learned on the bumpy ride, members of the group had found each other online, looking for others game to go off the beaten path.

They were from wildly different walks of life — a cook, a modeling agent, a tech reviewer, a human resources professional, a banker, a woman on a career hiatus and a chemical engineer. Xiaoyu Xu, the engineer, told me he had been to 110 countries, and was making his way through a list of 330 destinations.

Along the way, we got into a minor standoff with villagers over a Japanese tank along the side of the road. The tourists climbed onto the turret, and people from the surrounding village requested 100 kina, about $22. The group balked, and we got back on the road without paying.

“Yumi flow tasol,” I said back in the car, to the amusement of Luke Raupeto, our guide. The Tok Pisin phrase I’d picked up seemed fitting: Just go with it.

Around 2 p.m., the cars made an abrupt turn at a small trading hut. We’d arrived at an idyllic village with thatched roofs, lovingly tended flowers and cocoa beans laid out to dry.

We had reached Kokopo, a hamlet of a few dozen families, ready to begin the trek.

Leading us on the walk was the village chief, Robert Nunu. He said his father was among the people from the village who rushed to the crash site in 1943.

In the immediate aftermath of Admiral Yamamoto’s death, the account told in Japan was that he had perished as a dedicated soldier, found seated upright in the wreckage with a white-gloved hand on his sword. Mr. Nunu said his father had told a different story: that villagers had extracted the admiral badly burned, but still alive. He died later that day, he said.

Historical assessments of the Japanese admiral have also grown more complicated in the intervening years, as it became known how strongly he opposed going to war with the United States, and how he foresaw Japan’s eventual fate in the conflict.

Mr. Nunu was shirtless, in teal-colored galoshes with a machete as long as his arm. We would shortly come to see the wisdom of both. Within 10 minutes, we came across a knee-deep stream. I stripped off socks and boots and rolled up my pants, mosquitoes immediately flocking to my shins. At the next crossing, I gave in and waded, muddy stream water filling my boots, squishing and sloshing with each step. Yumi flow tasol.

A dozen people from Kokopo, including a couple of gleeful children, were along for the trek. We walked through potato fields and among pineapple plants. Our path soon became an overgrown blur of green. Every few steps, one of the villagers equipped with a machete hacked away at a banana leaf or a patch of tall grass.

None of the villagers, save for Mr. Nunu, wore shoes. One of the two women in the tourist group was in a miniskirt and white sneakers that didn’t stay white for long — the other, the agent, sported an orange crop top. (She finished the trek with no mosquito bites on her stomach. I asked.)

Mr. Xu, the engineer, brought three cameras in a large backpack, an action cam strapped to his chest, and a drone in another bag, which one of the villagers carried. The weight wasn’t too much trouble, he said. He’d been to Mount Everest.

After an hour and a half slogging through the vegetation, we came upon a small, unimpressive pile of metal. Don’t worry, this isn’t all of it, Mr. Raupeto said.

A minute later, we came to the main attraction: the crumbling fuselage of the plane, the engine that had broken apart and other fragments strewn through a glade surrounded by encroaching jungle.

Since 1984, the centennial of Admiral Yamamoto’s birth, members of the Yamamoto Admiration Society have been making pilgrimages to the wreck from his birthplace of Nagaoka. They held modest rites of remembrance, with sake and food placed atop a cloth draped over the plane’s remains. Some villagers carried the Japanese visitors piggyback across the streams, recalled Mathias Pihei, who was a regional administrator for the Buin District at the time and facilitated the visits during the 1980s.

“Through them I learned a lot about this man, Yamamoto,” said Mr. Pihei, 74. “As soon as we approached the crash site, they would shout, to greet the spirit.”

If his spirit was there with us, it didn’t make itself known. The tourists busied themselves taking photos of the aircraft, the engine, the interior of the fuselage, climbing the body to pose by the tail fin. The plane’s severed left wing, with the red sun of the Japanese flag, was missing. It was taken from the site to Nagaoka in the late 1980s, and now sits on display in a museum on Admiral Yamamoto. After about a half-hour, Mr. Raupeto started urging us to begin the trek back.

About halfway back, what had been sunny blue skies grew darker and fat droplets of rain started to fall. The villagers hacked off elephant ear fronds to use as umbrellas.

Roc He, 37, the tech reviewer, who has a following of more than 200,000 on Bilibili, one of China’s most popular video platforms, said he didn’t think most Chinese people would understand the desire to come to a place like Bougainville. They would say the money would be better spent on education or on children, he said. He had not told his parents about this trip.

As for the admiral and the plane wreckage, he said the Chinese generally had negative views of the Japanese in World War II, and it made him think about how far their war effort had reached.

I told him having grown up in South Korea myself, the history I was taught was predominantly concerned with the travails of having been colonized by the Japanese and our struggle for independence, and less with the battles far beyond our shores. Not unlike Bougainville, we had been at the mercy of land grabs by outsiders and their contests for dominion, with little heed for the fate of people living in these places.

It was nearly 6 p.m. by the time we were back at the cars. Vinsa Hu, the agent, had logged the return journey on her Apple Watch — 1.5 hours, 240 calories, 4 meters of elevation, 4.3 kilometers (2.7 miles).

Mr. Pihei, the former administrator, said he wished the plane were shielded from the elements so it could stand as a symbol with a message to visitors to Bougainville. The admiral may be associated with Japan’s wartime atrocities for many, but Mr. Pihei said that in the context of Bougainville, still reeling from its own war, the plane could stand for something different.

“When they see the plane, they see peace, because the person who died in the plane was a man of peace. He did not want war,” Mr. Pihei said. “Bougainville, too, does not war anymore. That plane and Bougainville are one. That’s the way I see it.”
